title: Knowledge Check 1 — Lessons 1-5
description: Pooled check over Lessons 1-5 of the AI at Work series. Score 80% or higher to unlock the cert prep practice exam.

questions.question: What is an LLM best described as?
options: A rules engine that follows pre-written instructions
A giant statistical prediction machine that predicts the next most likely token
A database of exact facts
A deterministic calculator
questions.explanation: Lesson 1: an LLM is a giant statistical prediction machine predicting the next token.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a model and automation?
options: Automation makes judgments; a model follows rules
A model makes judgments and is unpredictable, while automation executes pre-written rules
They are identical
A model never varies its output
questions.explanation: Lesson 1: a model applies judgment and is unpredictable; automation executes pre-written rules.

questions.question: How is an agent defined?
options: A single-turn chatbot
A model that takes multiple steps and uses tools to accomplish a goal
A pre-written automation
A model with no tools
questions.explanation: Lesson 1: an agent takes multiple steps and uses tools, unlike a plain single-response chatbot.

questions.question: Why do long AI replies tend to drift in quality?
options: The model gets tired
Each token is predicted probabilistically, so small errors accumulate
The model runs out of memory
The model stops predicting after a fixed length
questions.explanation: Lesson 2: probabilistic token prediction means small errors compound over a long reply.

questions.question: What is the context window?
options: Permanent memory of all past conversations
The amount of text, in tokens, the model can consider at any one time
The attachment file-size limit
The number of users on the tool
questions.explanation: Lesson 2: the context window is the amount of text, in tokens, the model can consider or remember at any one time.

questions.question: Which practice keeps load-bearing facts reliable in a long conversation?
options: Put important instructions near the end and restate critical facts
Never repeat instructions
Keep instructions only at the start
Ignore conversation length
questions.explanation: Lesson 2: put important instructions near the end and restate load-bearing facts.

questions.question: How is an AI hallucination defined?
options: A short, obviously broken sentence
Output that sounds plausible but is factually wrong or entirely fabricated
A rare error on obscure trivia only
A bug that will be patched
questions.explanation: Lesson 3: a hallucination sounds plausible but is factually wrong, irrelevant, or fabricated.

questions.question: Which is one shape a hallucination takes?
options: Answers always shorter than requested
Hallucinations can take the form of invented facts and fabricated sources.
Consistently correct answers
Refusals to answer
questions.explanation: Lesson 3: hallucinations include invented facts, fabricated sources, wrong specifics, and confident flat wrongness.

questions.question: Which habit helps catch hallucinations?
options: Only trust confident, assertive output
Ask the tool to show its work and express doubt about extras it adds
Never verify anything
Let the tool generate sources for you
questions.explanation: Lesson 3: catch hallucinations by checking only checkable things and asking the tool to show its work and doubt its extras.

questions.question: What core question should you ask before using AI for a task?
options: Am I asking for a draft, or am I asking for a decision?
Is the tool the cheapest vendor?
Is my prompt a full paragraph?
Is the output formatted as a table?
questions.explanation: Lesson 4: the core question is whether you are asking for a draft or a decision.

questions.question: Where does AI genuinely fail?
options: Drafting and rewriting
Single-right-answer facts, current/private information, and decisions with stakes
Summarizing documents
Explaining concepts
questions.explanation: Lesson 4: AI fails at single-right-answer facts, current or private info, and decisions with stakes.

questions.question: What is the core rule for anything typed into a public AI tool?
options: Assume the vendor cannot read it
Treat it as something the vendor could read and use later
Only enter data under 100 characters
Assume all tools are private
questions.explanation: Lesson 5: treat anything you type as readable by the vendor; all six major companies trained on user conversations by default.
